verdict.summary: ChunkedDecode parses the attacker-controlled chunk length with strtol and casts it to size_t without range/sign validation; an input like "-1" yields chunk_length = SIZE_MAX. With the wrap-admitted chunk_length = 2^64-1 from line 24 (attacker chunk text "-1"), writeBuffer + chunk_length is astronomically past end (line 10), so this byte write is also an out-of-bounds heap write on the same path; line 27's guard `p + 2 + chunk_length > end` does not exclude it because the sum wraps to a low address.

The required protective statement bounding start_line+height by s->avctx->height is absent; witness 65535 survives every shown guard.

Same unvalidated height (packet AV_RB16, line 34, 0..65535) and start_line-derived row_ptr (line 40) reach the 1bpp decoder, and no shown statement bounds them against s->avctx->height, admitting the same out-of-bounds row writes (CWE-787). Sibling sink of line 58; the missing fix is a start_line/height validation before the switch.

assumptions: reget_buffer (line 16) allocates s->frame planes sized to avctx->width/height, so avctx->height is the visible frame row capacity (line 38 uses it as the trusted height).

The qtrle_decode_*bpp helpers write up to `height` rows into s->frame as their standard decode contract; their bodies are unshown but the call-site arguments demonstrate the failing condition (wrapper-sink rule).
AV_PKT_DATA_PALETTE side data is AVPALETTE_SIZE bytes per standard API semantics; s->pal capacity is AVPALETTE_SIZE.
limitations: The signed multiplication `row_ptr = s->frame.linesize[0] * start_line;` (line 40) was considered for CWE-190 but linesize[0]'s value is not derivable in-fragment, so overflow is not confirmable (demoted).
The exact write offset/count inside the unshown decode helpers is inferred from the decode contract, not shown verbatim.
Capacity of s->frame.data[1] for the palette memcpy (line 82) is not shown; the copy uses the constant AVPALETTE_SIZE and is not part of the finding.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled XML with no <student> elements makes xmlXPathEvalExpression return an XPath object whose nodesetval is NULL; line 75 dereferences nodeset->nodeNr with no NULL check, crashing the process.

evidence.reason: nodeset is assigned from xpath_obj->nodesetval at line 74; the only prior guard, if(xpath_obj == NULL) at line 66, checks the object pointer and admits nodesetval == NULL. Per libxml2 standard semantics, an XPath expression whose node-set result is empty sets nodesetval to NULL, which attacker-controlled xml_data produces trivially (e.g., "<students/>"). Every guard on the path (lines 51, 58, 66) admits this state, so NULL reaches the dereference nodeset->nodeNr at line 75. The absent fix is a NULL/empty check such as 'if (nodeset == NULL) { ... return NULL; }' before the loop — CWE-476 NULL pointer dereference.

info->name is initialized to NULL at line 79 and copied at line 109 only when the matched <student> element contains a <name> child; an attacker can provide matching credentials with no <name>/<age>/<citizenship> children, so info->name/age/citizenship remain NULL. main's only guard, if(info) at line 157, admits these NULL fields, so printf("%s", ...) passes NULL for %s, which is undefined behavior per the C standard (glibc prints "(null)"). Secondary CWE-476 sink; the primary deciding sink is line 75.

assumptions: argv strings are NUL-terminated, so strlen(xml_data) at line 50 is bounded by the argument length.
libxml2 standard semantics: an XPath expression whose node-set result is empty yields xmlXPathObject.nodesetval == NULL; the literal expression "//student" always evaluates to a node-set.
xmlNodeSet::nodeTab has exactly nodeNr entries for i in [0, nodeNr), so nodeTab[i] at line 76 is in bounds when nodeset is non-NULL.
limitations: printf("%s", info->name) with NULL is tolerated by glibc (prints "(null)"), so the line 158-160 secondary sink is libc-dependent.
strdup(content) at lines 90/92/94 can only see NULL on xmlNodeGetContent allocation failure for an element node — not attacker-controlled under shown inputs; demoted.
The xmlNodeGetContent buffer is leaked in the name/age/citizenship branches (assigned via strdup without freeing content) — a memory-leak robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
nodeTab entries are assumed to be non-NULL matched element nodes per libxml2 node-set semantics; no NULL-producing path for nodeTab[i] is shown.

verdict.summary: The path-containment guard at line 36 admits sibling paths because it compares only the directory's realpath prefix without requiring a separator or NUL boundary, and it validates file_realpath while fopen at line 41 opens the unconstrained original file_path; an attacker-controlled filename containing ../ can escape dir_path and read an arbitrary accessible file.

evidence.reason: filename and dir_path are entry-point strings (argv[1]/argv[2] at line 73) with no shown validation. The only containment check, line 36 `if (strncmp(file_realpath, dir_realpath, strlen(dir_realpath)) != 0)`, admits any file_realpath whose first strlen(dir_realpath) bytes equal dir_realpath and never requires the following byte to be '/' or NUL; e.g. dir_realpath="/tmp/abc" (len 8) and file_realpath="/tmp/abc_evil/flag.txt" compare equal on the 8 compared bytes, so the guard passes. With file_path="/tmp/abc/../abc_evil/flag.txt", line 41 opens a file outside dir_path and its content is printed at line 75. The guard also constrains file_realpath, not the file_path actually consumed by fopen. The missing/mutated fix is the absent separator/NUL boundary test after the prefix. Primary CWE-22 path traversal; secondary CWE-697 incorrect comparison boundary. Witness admitted by every guard on the path (lines 21, 31, 36, 42).

assumptions: dir_path and filename are attacker-controlled entry-point strings (argv[1]/argv[2]) with no length or content validation in the fragment.
File paths resolve normally (no mount/namespace constraints shown) so sibling realpaths share the directory realpath prefix only via ../ traversal.
limitations: Unchecked realloc (lines 51, 59) NULL-on-OOM dereferences are not counted; no producing failure path is shown.
'char ch' / EOF signedness (line 50) can terminate reads early on bytes like 0xFF, which only truncates content, not a memory-safety issue.
Symlink swap TOCTOU between realpath (line 31) and fopen (line 41) requires a race and is not independently confirmed; it is additional exposure, not the deciding mechanism.

verdict.summary: create_dsa_key() calls mkstemp (line 22) but never checks fd or closes it. On failure (fd == -1, glibc leaves the template unchanged), param_filename is the literal '/tmp/tempXXXXXX' and the openssl commands at lines 27-28 create/overwrite a file at that attacker-predictable path in the world-writable /tmp directory, enabling symlink-following arbitrary file write. The missing protective statement is a status check on mkstemp's return value.

evidence.reason: The unchecked mkstemp result (line 22) leaves param_filename with the residual literal value '/tmp/tempXXXXXX' when fd == -1 (mkstemp's standard failure semantics, template unchanged on glibc). That value flows unguarded through snprintf (line 27) into system() at line 28, which runs 'openssl dsaparam -out /tmp/tempXXXXXX 1024' and creates or follows that predictable path. No guard on any path checks fd before this use; the absent fix is a status check such as 'if (fd == -1) return NULL;' plus close(fd), so the failure set is fully admitted. Primary CWE-377 (insecure/predictable temporary file); secondary CWE-59 (link following via a path an attacker can pre-create in /tmp).

assumptions: glibc leaves the mkstemp template buffer unchanged when mkstemp returns -1 (POSIX leaves its contents undefined on failure).
/tmp is world-writable so a local attacker can pre-create a file or symlink at the literal '/tmp/tempXXXXXX' path.
openssl -out opens its destination with open()-like semantics that follow symlinks.
limitations: mkstemp failure is environmental (e.g., EACCES/ENOSPC) and not directly attacker-triggerable, so the issue is a narrow-condition/low-severity insecure-temp-file flaw.
The dynamic read loop (lines 71-84) is fully protected: the 'if (total_read >= buffer_size)' resize at line 73 guarantees total_read < buffer_size at the null-terminator write, so no OOB there.
The unclosed fd from mkstemp is only a resource leak, not itself a security finding.

verdict.summary: User-controlled filename is concatenated into file_path with no validation and passed to fopen, so a name containing '/' or '..' (e.g., '../../../etc/passwd') reads any process-readable file outside the intended directory.

evidence.reason: filename (entry-point argv[1]) retains its full string domain because no shown statement constrains it; line 20 concatenates dir_path + '/' + filename into file_path via snprintf without rejecting '/', '..', or absolute names, and fopen (line 23) consumes that unchecked path. The protective statement required to cover this failure set (e.g., if (strchr(filename, '/') != NULL) return empty_result; before path construction) is absent, so a witness such as "../../../etc/passwd" reaches fopen on every path, enabling arbitrary process-readable file reads outside dir_path (CWE-22).

assumptions: filename and dir_path are entry-point (argv) inputs with no shown constraint; fopen follows standard OS path resolution including '..' and absolute paths.
file_path (line 19) is a 1024-byte stack buffer, so snprintf (line 20) cannot overflow it.
limitations: NULL-deref candidates at lines 34 and 42 (and malloc at line 18) depend on OOM failure of realloc/malloc and are not attacker-triggerable via a shown channel; demoted.
snprintf truncation at line 20 only shortens the path and cannot expand attacker reach.
Plain-char signedness for ch (line 31) is implementation-defined and yields at most early termination or a DoS, not a confirmed memory-safety issue.

verdict.summary: get_codec_data dereferences AVStream *vst on the NUV_EXTRADATA/'R' path even though the entry guard `if (!vst && !myth)` admits vst==NULL whenever myth is nonzero, and passes an unvalidated file-derived size to av_malloc/get_buffer; a crafted NUV frame (with NULL vst or a huge/negative size) triggers a NULL-pointer dereference.

evidence.reason: Sink dereferences vst; the only prior guard, line 4 `if (!vst && !myth) return 1;`, admits vst==NULL whenever myth!=0 (operator `&&` under-excludes the NULL state the sink needs), and lines 10/14 admit file-controlled NUV_EXTRADATA/'R'. The MYTHEXT branch's own `if (vst)` at line 29 confirms vst may legitimately be NULL. No shown statement excludes vst==NULL on this path, so the failure set reaches line 15 unexcluded — CWE-476; the protective form is an unconditional vst exclusion (e.g., `||` instead of `&&` or an added `if (vst)` check), and the shown guard is the mutated/insufficient form.

size is assigned at line 13 from file bytes via get_le32 with no validation on this path; av_malloc(size) at line 16 returns NULL under standard NULL-on-failure semantics for negative/huge values, and get_buffer then writes `size` bytes through NULL (also re-dereferencing a NULL vst). Guards at lines 4 and 14 constrain only vst/myth and subtype, never size; a needed `if (size < 0)`-class check is absent — CWE-476.

assumptions: get_le32 returns an unsigned 32-bit file-derived value, and av_malloc/get_buffer follow standard NULL-on-failure / read-into-buffer semantics.
The NUV container bytes (frametype, subtype, sizes) are entry-point-derived content (provenance 2(a)), so the attacker can choose the 'R' sub-branch.
limitations: PKTSIZE's macro body is not shown; the negative/huge-size witness relies on its standard shift/multiply-by-4 semantics, so the size-driven NULL deref is secondary to the vst NULL-deref finding.
url_fskip(pb, size) with a possibly negative default-case size (line 56) is demoted: backward-seek behavior is not shown to corrupt memory.
Callers of get_codec_data are unshown; the verdict rests on the shown guard at line 4 admitting vst==NULL with myth!=0, not on any assumed caller state.

verdict.summary: The temporary file is created via the predictable tmpnam() name and opened with fopen(..., "w"), which follows any pre-existing symlink at that path, allowing an attacker to redirect the write to an arbitrary file (TOCTOU/symlink overwrite). No protective statement (e.g. mkstemp/O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW) constrains this sink.

evidence.reason: filename is derived from tmpnam() at line 21, an entry-point/untrusted-environment controlled, predictable /tmp path that the fragment never protects. fopen(filename,"w") follows any symlink an attacker pre-places at that path, so a privileged or victim write can be redirected to an arbitrary file. The failure set (attacker-chosen target via link following) is fully admitted: the only guards present (NULL checks on strdup/fopen/fputs/fclose at lines 23/28/33/39) never constrain the path or its link. The absent fix is the safe sink substitution to mkstemp() with O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW, whose mutated/missing form leaves the race fully admitted. Primary CWE-377 with secondary CWE-59 link-following.

tmpnam() generates a globally predictable temporary filename in the shared directory with no exclusive-creation guarantee. This is the insecure name producer feeding fopen(filename,"w") at line 27; the missing protective statement is exclusive/link-safe creation, leaving the failure set (predictable-name symlink race) admitted. Same root mechanism as the primary sink.

assumptions: results (argv[1]) is a plain data string written via fputs and is not involved in the vulnerability.
tmpnam() resolves to a predictable path in the shared temporary directory, per its standard semantics.
The NULL/EOF/close status checks (lines 23/28/33/39) are correct and are not the failing mechanism.
limitations: The specific attacker write target depends on the OS temp directory and the process's privileges; the confirmed mechanism is the link-following race inherent to tmpnam()+fopen.
A fully race-free fix would require mkstemp (or O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW), which is absent from the fragment.

verdict.summary: The only candidate sink is qemu_coroutine_enter(co), which could fail only on co == NULL; no shown statement produces or admits NULL (opaque is a framework-supplied callback parameter with no shown call site), and any dereference occurs inside the unshown callee, so the NULL-dereference candidate is demoted and no confirmed vulnerability exists.

The candidate is demoted because CWE-476 requires a NULL value produced or admitted by shown statements and a shown dereference on that path: opaque is a framework-supplied callback parameter with no shown call site, and the dereference is inside the unshown qemu_coroutine_enter body, which cannot serve as a producer of a failing value in either direction.

The qemu_coroutine_enter callee body is unshown, so standard NULL-on-failure or dereference semantics for it are not established within the fragment.
No entry-point, size, index, or format-string channels exist in this fragment; no other dangerous operation was identified.

verdict.summary: File-derived `size` (line 13) is unvalidated before `av_malloc(size)` (line 16) and an immediate `get_buffer` write (line 17); there is no size bound and no NULL check on the allocation, so a huge/negative admitted size that fails allocation yields a NULL-pointer write.

The only guard on the path, `if (vst && subtype == 'R')` at line 14, constrains `vst` and `subtype` but not `size` or the malloc result, so it admits the witness `size = 0x7FFFFFFF`; when the allocation returns NULL (standard av_malloc failure semantics), `get_buffer` writes to NULL. The named absent fix is the missing size bound / malloc-result NULL check; primary mechanism is a NULL-pointer write (CWE-476).

assumptions: PKTSIZE is not shown, so `size` keeps the full int range of the get_le32-derived value (no masking assumed).
av_malloc has standard NULL-on-failure semantics; get_buffer writes up to `size` bytes, so capacity equals `size` when the allocation succeeds.
pb is an entry-point byte stream whose header fields (lines 13, 25, 53) are attacker-controlled absent a shown bound.
limitations: The NULL write at line 17 is demonstrable on the allocation-failure path; if the allocator satisfies the huge request, only excessive allocation/consumption occurs within this fragment (downstream extradata use is outside the shown code).
url_fskip calls (lines 46, 56) only seek forward and have no memory-corruption failure set; the line 26 equality guard renders the line 46 skip PRESENT.
NULL states for vst->codec / ast->codec have no producer in the shown fragment and were not treated as findings.

verdict.summary: secure_decrypt is called at line 15 with header->file_size as the byte count, and header->file_size is an unvalidated field of decrypted, untrusted header data. No shown guard (line 7 decrypt status, line 11 magic equality) bounds file_size against the remaining buffer capacity, so an attacker-influenced oversized file_size is passed to secure_decrypt, causing out-of-bounds access past the file region.

evidence.reason: header->file_size originates from the decrypted header (untrusted: the fragment validates header->magic at line 11 but nothing constrains file_size) and its full declared domain is admitted by the guards on the path (line 7 and line 11 constrain only decrypt status and magic). It is consumed at line 15 as the process/decrypt length for the buffer at file (line 14), with no capacity bound check before the call. The absent fix is a bound check such as 'if (header->file_size > (capacity - sizeof(*header))) goto secure_wipe_keys;'; its absence is the ABSENT resolution, with the surviving witness being any file_size value that exceeds the bytes remaining after the header, yielding an out-of-bounds read/write (CWE-787) in secure_decrypt.

assumptions: The file region (file at line 14) is bounded by the finite object that data points to, so a file_size exceeding the remaining bytes is an out-of-bounds access.
secure_decrypt processes (reads ciphertext and writes decrypted plaintext for) the byte count given as its second argument.
Decrypted header contents are untrusted input because the fragment itself validates header->magic before trusting the header.
limitations: The exact capacity of the data object is not literal in the fragment, so the arithmetic of the overflow cannot be shown numerically.
The body of secure_decrypt is not shown; standard decryption semantics (process file_size bytes in place) are assumed.
A NULL-data dereference at line 11 was not counted: no shown statement produces or admits NULL for data.

verdict.summary: pipePath (std::string, no shown length bound) is copied by strncpy into sun_path using the full buffer size, so a path of length >= sizeof(remote.sun_path) (108 on Linux) leaves sun_path without a NUL terminator; the subsequent AF_UNIX ::connect consumes sun_path as a string, reading past the terminated path, because no length check, -1 size, or explicit terminator write is present.

evidence.reason: pipePath derives from endpoint.name() (line 4), a std::string with unbounded domain and no shown length constraint; strncpy copies sizeof(remote.sun_path) bytes, the capacity shown at this same line, and by standard strncpy semantics writes no NUL when the source length is >= the bound. The missing/mutated fix is the -1 size (or an explicit sun_path[sizeof(remote.sun_path)-1] = '\0', or a length guard); the admitted witness is pipePath.size() == sizeof(remote.sun_path) (108 bytes), which leaves sun_path[107] nonzero and unterminated, causing CWE-170 missing string termination and, via the line 15 connect consumer, a CWE-125 over-read.

Sinks the sockaddr built at lines 10-11: AF_UNIX connect consumes remote.sun_path as a NUL-terminated path per standard API semantics, but for any pipePath of length >= sizeof(remote.sun_path) the buffer was never terminated (line 11 copies the full size and no terminator statement exists). The failing value (unterminated sun_path) is admitted by every shown guard — none of lines 17, 44, or 52 constrain the path length — so this resolution is ABSENT: the over-read is enabled by the missing termination fix at line 11.

assumptions: sockaddr_un::sun_path capacity equals sizeof(remote.sun_path) as used at line 11 (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS).
pipePath is a std::string whose declared domain has no shown length bound.
FATAL_FAIL aborts on failure, so the fd/errno checks (lines 8, 17-33, 49-50) are not protective for the path-length failure set.
limitations: endpoint is an internal-helper parameter with no shown call site, so the triggering input is attributed via the string type's unbounded domain rather than a visible attacker channel.
select()'s discarded return at line 42 was examined but not treated as a finding: its FD_ISSET-false path closes the fd and returns -1, yielding no demonstrated memory-safety or security failure.
The exact over-read extent depends on the OS kernel's AF_UNIX path lookup, whose body is unshown; the finding stands on the shown API contract misuse (unterminated sun_path passed to connect).

verdict.summary: Every dangerous operation with a failure set derivable from the shown code is protected: the L6-7 guard excludes the NULL failure of lock_user_struct from every rt_sf dereference, the L8-9 guard excludes any nonzero do_setcontext status before the success path, and the do_sigaltstack address is a compile-time offset inside the region already validated at L6, so its discarded status has no producible failing value.

evidence.reason: Decisive protective statement for the only failure value the fragment can produce: lock_user_struct returns 0 and leaves rt_sf NULL on lock failure (standard semantics), and this guard excludes exactly that value from every path that dereferences rt_sf at line 8 (&rt_sf->uc), derives the do_sigaltstack address (lines 10-12), or unlocks it (lines 13/16). Identity (same variable, no intervening assignment), reach (single path, always executed), and exactness (! plus goto covering the NULL failure with no off-by-one) all hold; it survives the single-statement diff audit because removing the check or its negation would admit rt_sf == NULL at line 8.

Second protective statement: the nonzero failure status of do_setcontext is excluded by goto sigsegv before do_sigaltstack (line 10) and the success-path unlock (line 13) execute, so a guest ucontext rejected by do_setcontext cannot proceed to the altstack restore or the success-path unlock.

assumptions: QEMU standard semantics of lock_user_struct/lock_user: on failure it returns 0 and leaves the out-pointer NULL, and on success it validates a region of sizeof(*rt_sf) bytes at rt_sf_addr.

tuc_stack is a member of target_ucontext, which is a member of target_rt_sigframe (as shown by the offsetof expression at line 11), so rt_sf_addr + offsetof(struct target_rt_sigframe, uc.tuc_stack) lies strictly inside the region validated at line 6.
QEMU unlock_user is NULL-safe by standard semantics.
limitations: The bodies of do_setcontext, do_sigaltstack, and unlock_user_struct are unshown; their internal behavior can neither add nor remove a confirmed failure under the evidence standards.

The do_sigaltstack return is discarded (later upstream replaced the call with target_restore_altstack over an already-verified host pointer), but no failing value is producible on any shown path because the address is inside the line-6-validated region; any residual effect would be guest-visible only, not host memory corruption.
The guest-layout constant SIGNAL_FRAMESIZE + 16 (line 5) is not tied to any shown capacity or bounds check, so it cannot ground a finding in either direction.
Membership of the pair was not used; the verdict rests solely on the per-sink resolution of the shown fragment.

verdict.summary: The user-supplied filename is concatenated with dir_path at line 19 and opened at line 22 without any path-containment or traversal validation, allowing reads of arbitrary files outside the intended directory.

evidence.reason: filename originates from argv[1] (entry-point input, unconstrained) and reaches file_path = dir_path + "/" + filename at line 19, then the open at line 22. The only guard, `if (!file.is_open())` at line 23, checks OS open failure and does not constrain the path's location, so the admitted witness filename = "/etc/passwd" (or "../../etc/passwd") is opened and its content returned. The absent fix is any containment/validation check on filename (rejecting separators, "..", or absolute prefixes, or verifying a canonical path prefix) before the sink. Mechanism: CWE-22 path traversal enabling arbitrary file disclosure.

assumptions: dir_path and filename are both attacker-controlled command-line inputs, so the harm is confinement of the read to dir_path.
Standard OS/path resolution semantics apply: a leading "/" or "../" segment in the joined path resolves outside dir_path.
limitations: The is_open() check at line 23 mitigates unreadable/nonexistent files but is not a path-containment guard and does not affect the verdict.
No memory-safety, format-string, or status-handling sinks exist in the fragment; traversal is the sole confirmed mechanism.

verdict.summary: celt_denormalize indexes fixed band tables (block->energy, ff_celt_mean_energy, ff_celt_freq_bands, ff_celt_freq_range) with i ranging over the unvalidated [f->start_band, f->end_band) interval, and writes dst[j] with a size-influenced j; no band-limit check such as 'i < ff_celt_bands_end' exists, so an out-of-range i causes OOB reads and a potential OOB write.

The same unguarded i selects ff_celt_freq_range[i] at line 8 and computes dst at line 5; j spans [0, ff_celt_freq_range[i] << f->size) with f->size unvalidated, so the write dst[j] *= norm at line 9 falls outside the destination once i is beyond the band table (the identical missing band-limit fix), an OOB write (CWE-787).

assumptions: block->energy and the ff_celt_* band tables hold one entry per CELT band, so any index at or beyond the band count is out of range; the absent fix's boundary constant (ff_celt_bands_end) would name that count.
f->start_band, f->end_band, and f->size are decode-state values not constrained anywhere in the fragment; no caller validation is assumed.
limitations: The exact numeric capacities of the band tables and the data buffer are not written in the fragment; the line 9 write is secondary because data's capacity is unshown, though it shares the same missing bound.
FFMIN(log_norm, 32.0f) clamps only the exponent, not any index or size, and is not a protective statement for these sinks.
If an unshown caller validated f->end_band before this call, the OOB would be blocked; per the evidence rules no such external invariant is credited.

verdict.summary: Every dangerous operation carries a protective statement: the vec-building loop is bounded because line 42 (len = args->len = max_blocksize) clamps the attacker-supplied len whenever count > max_blocksize, and line 20 forces count == len, so len never exceeds svc_max_payload; decode_fh is NULL-checked at lines 10-11.

evidence.reason: Protective statement for the rq_vec/rq_pages[v] indexing sink. len is attacker-derived (ntohl(*p++) at line 16, u32 domain), but line 20 forces len == count, and when count > max_blocksize this clamp assigns max_blocksize to the exact local len consumed at lines 47-53; when count <= max_blocksize, len == count <= max_blocksize. Every surviving path therefore admits only len in [0, max_blocksize]; the witness len in (max_blocksize, 2^32-1] that would drive v past the rq_vec/rq_pages capacity is excluded. Removing or mutating this assignment (e.g. only args->count = max_blocksize) leaves len unclamped and reaches the line 50 indexed write out of bounds.

The dangerous loop-carried indexed write. Its index v is derived only from len, which line 42 (clamp to max_blocksize) and line 20 (count == len) bound to [0, max_blocksize], so v cannot exceed ceil(max_blocksize/PAGE_SIZE)+1, i.e. the server-sanctioned payload pages; line 37 additionally guarantees received bytes (dlen >= XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4) cover the claimed length. No out-of-bounds witness survives the guards, so this sink resolves PRESENT.

assumptions: max_blocksize = svc_max_payload(rqstp) is the server-side maximum payload and the RPC layer supplies at least that many pages in rq_pages for an accepted request.
rq_vec and rq_pages capacities are not declared in the fragment; the safe verdict rests on the line 42 clamp keeping len within svc_max_payload.
limitations: The absolute capacities of rq_vec and rq_pages are not visible in the fragment; the not-vulnerable verdict depends on the svc-layer invariant that a payload of max_blocksize fits in the provided pages.
The untrusted word reads at lines 14-16 are not flagged because no head-buffer capacity is derivable from the fragment (XDR decoder precondition, not a shown failure).
count/len values above max_blocksize are dead witnesses: they are clamped at line 42 before reaching the loop.

verdict.summary: In the non-downmix branch, the sink `dst[n] += (src[n] + round) >> shift;` performs the compound addition in signed int without the required `(unsigned)` cast, so a bitstream-derived `dst[n]` near INT32_MAX plus a positive shifted residual overflows int (UB). evidence.reason: Line 52 is the deciding sink: `dst[n]` (`c->bands[0].msb_sample_buffer[ch]`, bitstream-derived, no shown clamp) keeps the full int32 residual range after every guard on the path (line 15 constrains only the trip count via `nsamples == dca->core.npcmsamples`; line 31 admits `spkr >= 0`; line 37 admits `shift <= 24`). `round <= 1<<23` and `(src[n]+round)>>shift` yields a positive value (e.g., 6298923 with shift=0), so `dst[n] + RHS` overflows int when `dst[n] > INT32_MAX - RHS`, e.g. 2147286116 + 6298923 = 2153585039 > 2147483647 — signed overflow (CWE-190). Line 37 enforces `shift <= 24` and line 41 evaluates `1 << (shift - 1)` only for `shift > 0`, so `shift - 1 <= 23` and the line 41 shift is defined.
